sections.synopsis: Precipitation will linger today as a weak system brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the mountains. A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation this Saturday. An active weather pattern resumes next week with a series of systems moving across Western Washington.
sections.short_term:
Latest radar imagery shows precipitation continues to fill in from the south as a shortwave trough traverses Western Washington, bringing light lowland rain and mountain snow. Expecting precipitation to linger into the late afternoon hours, before conditions dry out tonight. Drier conditions Saturday as a weak upper-level ridge builds over the Pacific Northwest. Light to calm winds tonight into Saturday morning and residual moisture from recent rain will help promote fog development across portions of Western Washington, with highest confidence (70-90% chance) over the southern interior. As for Puget Sound, there is a 25-40% chance, with higher chances in the river valleys. Fog expected to dissipate by the afternoon, however skies will remain overcast as mid and high level clouds move into the area. The ridge axis will push east of the area on Sunday.

A developing low pressure system offshore will bring some rain inland across Western Washington on Sunday. Parts of Western Washington will likely see windy conditions developing by Sunday night, but the path of the low will define a lot of the details.

Coastal flooding remains a threat for many areas heading into the weekend. Areas along the north interior coastline are favored to see the highest degree of coastal flooding over the weekend, with lesser impacts expected elsewhere.
sections.long_term:
Models continue to struggle on the exact path of the low pressure system, which could have significant implications in terms of the wind forecast. The latest GFS continues to take a weakening low into British Columbia, while the latest ECMWF has a 980 mb low making landfall towards Western Washington. Shall the low follow the GFS projected path, the strongest winds will stay primarily confined to the coast. However, shall the low follow the ECMWF, the low will bring the strongest winds towards the interior.

Ensembles hint at quieter weather towards the middle of the week with an upper-level ridge building and the storm track shifting into California.

Additional coastal flooding may occur into next week due to high astronomical tides, with highest concern on Monday.
sections.marine:
Winds will remain lighter through Saturday morning as a weak weather system moves into Oregon tonight. East winds develop Saturday afternoon and continue through Sunday, before becoming more southeast Sunday night ahead of the next storm system. Localized Small Craft Advisory wind gusts may occur Saturday night, and especially on Sunday along the western entrance of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and southern coastal waters.

A strengthening weather system moves northwards across the Northeast Pacific Sunday and into the Coastal Waters on Monday. Uncertainty continues in regards to the exact track and strength of this weather system. At this time, south winds are expected to peak on Monday. Probabilities show 75 to 95% chance for gale force wind gusts over the Coastal Waters on Monday, with probabilities of 40 to 70% for the interior waters. Winds are expected to be strongest along the coastal waters, and there is a 20 to 40% probability for Storm force wind gusts during this period as well. Winds begin to ease on Tuesday, but remain elevated at times through the week as additional weather systems are possible.

Seas subside below 10 feet tonight, ranging 5 to 8 feet Saturday and Sunday. Seas will increase with the next system on Monday, ranging 15 to 18 feet. JD

sections.synopsis: Winds will veer towards standard ENE trade wind direction tomorrow. Temperatures and humidities will rise slightly Sunday as cold air advection begins to dwindle. An upper level trough and associated surface trough may develop west of the state late Sunday into Tuesday. This may provide a potential uptick in shower activity.
sections.prev_discussion:
Issued at 347 PM HST Fri Nov 27 2026

Satellite and radar shows scattered cumulus clouds with light precipitation being advected over windward and mountain areas by N-NNE winds. Some terrain sheltered areas such as the Kona slopes of Big Island have also developed some cloud cover, but with no discernible precipitation. Expect showers to remain primarily focused over windward and mountain areas with a slight uptick in shower activity tonight.

Winds have begun to veer today, and are expected to reach a typical ENE trade wind direction with moderate speeds by tomorrow. As the winds veer, the cold air advection will decrease, causing humidity and temperatures to slightly increase by Sunday onward.

An upper level trough and associated surface trough are expected to develop just west of the state late Sunday into Tuesday, bringing a higher likelihood of showers. Global models as of now are in general agreement that most of the instability and higher moisture content will remain west of the state, with Kauai and Oahu likely seeing most of the showers. Confidence in this will grow with time as we get closer to next week. Easterly trade winds will be primarily moderate to breezy Monday onward as migrating high pressure builds and moves NE of the islands.
sections.marine:
High pressure will become firmly established to the northwest of the state tonight into tomorrow, causing winds to veer to the northeast and decrease into the moderate to locally fresh range through Sunday morning. A fading extra-large north-northwest swell is keeping a Small Craft Advisory in place for primarily windward coastal waters for seas above 10 ft through tonight as the extra large north-northwest swell declines. By Sunday evening, trade winds increase to locally strong as the high to the northwest moves closer to the islands and a broad surface trough forms to the west of the islands. This trough will also cause the trade winds to veer further to the east. Around this same time, an upper level trough could move over the western half of the state, increasing showers and possibly isolated thunderstorms for western waters. By the middle of next week, models indicate trade winds decreasing as a front passes far to the north and weakens the high. This could then be followed by restrengthening as the high re-intensifies.

An extra-large north-northwest (330 to 350 degree) swell has been gradually fading, and a high surf advisory for north facing shores of all islands is now in place through 6 am Saturday. The west-facing shores were dropped from an advisory due to the fact that as the northwest swell has been declining, the swell has been becoming more northerly. The swell will fade further through the weekend, with surf dropping below advisory levels by Saturday morning. A small to moderate northwest swell arrives late Sunday and peaks on Monday, then fades through mid-week. A larger long period northwest swell follows this, arriving Wednesday and peaking during the latter half of next week.

Surf heights along east-facing shores will continue to be elevated tonight due to wrapping from the north-northwest swell. As the swell fades, a medium-period northeast swell generated by a storm- force low to the northeast of the islands will keep surf elevated for east-facing shores through Sunday. More typical, short- period trade wind swell will return by Monday. Surf along south- facing shores will remain tiny to small tonight, with a small bump possible this weekend, followed by a return to background small to flat levels next week.
